title: Wendell and the Portrait
premise: Juniper Eriksen returns to the village of Hallowmere to bury their twin brother Wendell, only to find the death certificate names Juniper instead — and the portrait above the family hearth now shows a face that is neither twin's. When the church bell that was melted down in 1911 begins to ring at dusk each night, the villagers start counting: every toll marks one soul the portrait has claimed, and it is owed one hundred before it will rest. Juniper, who documents everything as a form of prayer, discovers Wendell's hidden notebooks revealing he struck a bargain with the portrait to save their dying mother — a bargain that traded one twin for the family's survival, and the portrait has come to collect the balance. To break the count, Juniper must choose between destroying the portrait and losing everyone it has already taken, or completing Wendell's bargain and surrendering themself; in the end they burn the portrait at the hundredth toll, freeing the taken souls but erasing every record, photograph, and memory of Wendell — so Juniper writes his name in the ashes and carries the only version of him that remains.
about_author: Felix Lockridge is the pen name of a former parish archivist who spent a decade cataloguing funeral records in coastal Norwegian villages before turning to fiction. They write horror about grief, ledgers, and the things families agree not to say out loud.

chapters.title: The Wrong Name on the Stone
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper arrives in Hallowmere for Wendell's funeral and finds the grave marker, the death certificate, and the priest's records all name Juniper Eriksen instead. The villagers greet them with pity, as if they are the ghost. Emotional beat: disorientation and the first crack in Juniper's faith that documents tell the truth.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper moves into the family house, photographing and cataloguing Wendell's belongings as a coping ritual. They find Wendell's room untouched but subtly wrong — dust everywhere except a clean path from bed to hearth, where the old family portrait hangs. Emotional beat: grief expressed as control, and the first unease.

chapters.title: The Face in the Oil Paint
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Studying the portrait — a stern ancestor painted in 1911, the year the bell was melted — Juniper realizes the painted face shifts between sittings: sometimes Wendell, sometimes themself, sometimes no one they know. Their mother, half-lucid, begs them not to look at it after dark. Emotional beat: creeping dread.

chapters.title: A Bell That Was Never Cast
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV, with neighbor Astrid Vold. At dusk the church bell rings — but parish records, which Astrid keeps, confirm it was melted for scrap in 1911. Only Juniper, Astrid, and the children seem to hear it. Emotional beat: the horror becomes communal and undeniable.

chapters.title: Wendell's Notebooks
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Hidden beneath the floorboards, Juniper finds Wendell's meticulous notebooks: he documented a bargain he made with the portrait — one twin's life in exchange for their mother's recovery from her long illness. The final entry reads: 'It does not care which twin. It only cares that the count reaches one hundred.' Emotional beat: betrayal and heartbreak.

chapters.title: The Count Begins
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. The bell tolls once at dusk; that night, the blacksmith's eldest son is found dead, his face smoothed blank like wet paint. Astrid counts the parish's old deaths and realizes the portrait has claimed ninety-seven souls across a century — it is nearly full. Emotional beat: cold arithmetic of terror.

chapters.title: What the Mother Knows
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper confronts their mother, now mysteriously healthy, and extracts the truth: she knew of the bargain and let Wendell make it. She begs Juniper to finish it — one twin for the family, as the portrait demands — because she cannot lose the family's luck. Emotional beat: love against duty, mother against child.

chapters.title: Ninety-Eight
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Two tolls in one night. Astrid finds the second victim — the priest who misnamed the grave — and in his office discovers a 1911 ledger: the original parish priest made the first bargain, trading his congregation's bell for the village's survival during the famine. Emotional beat: justice outside the law has a long, rotten history here.

chapters.title: The Portrait's Terms
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. The portrait speaks — not in words, but in images Juniper's camera captures: Wendell alive inside the paint, and a hundred small figures pressed beneath the varnish. Destroying the portrait destroys them all. Completing the count frees them and takes Juniper. Emotional beat: the price of survival made explicit.

chapters.title: Evacuation
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid and Juniper try to move the remaining villagers out of Hallowmere before the hundredth toll, but the road loops back on itself and the ferryman charges a price no one can pay twice. Some villagers refuse to leave, bound by old bargains of their own. Emotional beat: futility and solidarity.

chapters.title: Ninety-Nine
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. The ninety-ninth victim is Astrid's grandson, taken from a locked room. Astrid, shattered, turns on Juniper: 'It wanted you from the start. Wendell only delayed it.' The village turns, gently, terribly, toward Juniper as the answer. Emotional beat: betrayal by a friend, isolation.

chapters.title: The Twin in the Glass
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Mirrors begin showing Wendell instead of Juniper. In the strongest reflection, Wendell communicates: he has been holding the count at ninety-nine from inside, refusing to let the last soul be taken, but his grip is failing. He begs Juniper not to come after him. Emotional beat: love against duty, twin against twin.

chapters.title: The Ferryman's Price
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid, seeking redemption, finds the ferryman — the portrait's original sitter, kept alive a century past his death — and learns the loophole: the count can be broken not by a soul given, but by a soul freely refused by the one it was taken from. Emotional beat: desperate hope with a terrible cost.

chapters.title: What Juniper Documents
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper spends a day recording everything — the house, the village, their own face, a letter to whoever comes after — knowing the destruction of the portrait may erase all records, including Wendell's existence. Documentation as prayer, one last time. Emotional beat: elegiac calm before the storm.

chapters.title: The Mother's Choice
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper offers their mother the truth one final time: confess the bargain publicly and the portrait loses its claim, because it feeds on unspoken debt. The mother refuses, choosing the family's comfort over its soul. Emotional beat: the theme of love against duty turned inside out.

chapters.title: Ninety-Nine and Holding
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. The bell tolls erratically, straining, as the portrait tries to take the hundredth soul and Wendell holds it back from within. The paint begins to blister and weep. The village's remaining bargain-bound residents begin to age rapidly as their debts come due. Emotional beat: the dam is cracking.

chapters.title: Into the Varnish
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Against Wendell's plea, Juniper cuts their palm and presses it to the canvas, crossing into the portrait to reach their twin. Inside: a grey village of the taken, ninety-nine souls, Wendell at the center holding the door shut. Emotional beat: love that refuses the terms of survival.

chapters.title: The Hundredth Toll Refused
chapters.summary: Juniper and Wendell's alternating POV. Juniper finds Wendell and offers to take his place holding the count; Wendell refuses — and in refusing freely, breaks the loophole open. The hundredth toll rings and finds no one willing to be taken. The portrait begins to burn from within. Emotional beat: climax; the count broken by refusal, not sacrifice.

chapters.title: Ash on the Hearth
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. From outside, Astrid watches the portrait consume itself and the house with it. The bell falls silent forever. The taken souls pass through the village as light and are gone. The surviving family is pulled from the fire. Emotional beat: release, awe, and the first clean silence in a century.

chapters.title: The Erasure
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. The price reveals itself: every record, photograph, and memory of Wendell is gone — even Juniper's mother cannot say who they buried. Only Juniper remembers, because Juniper held the documentation in their own hands at the moment of burning. Emotional beat: grief without a grave, survival without witness.

chapters.title: A Name Written in Ashes
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper carves WENDELL ERIKSEN into the hearthstone with a knife, then begins a new notebook — the first entry his name, his story, everything Juniper alone remembers. Their mother, sensing something lost she cannot name, weeps at the kitchen table. Emotional beat: mourning transformed into testimony.

chapters.title: The Bell That Stays Silent
chapters.summary: Juniper and Astrid's alternating POV. Months later, Juniper leaves Hallowmere, carrying the notebook; Astrid stays to keep the parish records honest, adding a page for the ninety-nine and the one who held the door. The church bell tower stands empty, and at dusk, Juniper listens — and hears nothing at all. Emotional beat: hard-won peace, and the choice to keep remembering.
